notes.title: Start here: Pulse writes its analytics semantics down as contracts
notes.body:
Pulse is a product-analytics platform: an SDK sends events, an ingest service accepts them, and query code turns them into funnels, experiments and sampled charts. This quest is about the places where a number could quietly mean two different things, and how Pulse pins each one down in writing.

Read in this order. `docs/funnel-semantics.md` is the funnel contract for analysts; keep `packages/insights/src/funnel.ts` open beside it. Then ADR-0011 and `docs/experiments/peeking.md` cover how users are assigned to variants and how an experiment is judged; the code is `packages/shared/src/bucketing.ts`, `packages/flags/src/evaluate.ts` and `packages/flags/src/results.ts`. Finish with three short ADRs: 0003 (API keys), 0009 (the live tail) and 0010 (sampling).

Most questions give you a small timeline or a setting and ask what the code does. Trace the code line by line rather than guessing from the doc wording.

excerpts.quote: A funnel query is a **contract**: "conversion" has to mean exactly one thing, or two people run the same funnel

readMore.why: The single-pass funnel state machine; about 60 lines carry every funnel rule.
Why assignment is a hash and why the analysis uses a fixed horizon.

notes.title: Concept: a funnel is a tiny state machine per person
notes.body:
`computeFunnel` turns a list of events into step counts. It groups events by person and then walks each person's events with a couple of local variables: `level` (how many steps are done) and `anchor` (a timestamp the window is measured from).

Treat it as a tiny state machine and trace it by hand. Write down, for each event, which branch of the loop it takes. Pin down four things from the code rather than from the contract page: the order the events are walked in, the exact moment `anchor` is assigned (and whether it can ever be reassigned), what the window check compares the event time against and with which operator, and what happens to an event that matches a step out of order.

Then read the last lines of the loop to see how a person's final `level` turns into counts per step. `computeFunnelBreakdown` sits next to it: note how it decides which group a person belongs to, and whether it sorts first.

excerpts.quote: ## What a funnel counts
let level = 0; // steps completed so far

readMore.why: The five numbered rules the code implements.

notes.title: Concept: assigning variants with a hash instead of a table
notes.body:
Pulse assigns users to flag variants with a hash instead of an assignment table. Every evaluator (the server, the SDK and backfill jobs) calls `bucket(...)` in `packages/shared/src/bucketing.ts`, which hashes a string with FNV-1a, finishes it with murmur3's fmix32 mixer and divides by 2^32 to land in [0, 1). Same inputs give the same number on every machine, with no database and no communication.

While reading, work out for yourself exactly what goes into the hashed string and why each part is there. Then read `evaluateFlag` in `packages/flags/src/evaluate.ts` top to bottom and list its checks in the order they run, with the reason string each early return gives. Note how many times it calls `bucket` and with which salts. Finally, take one user and a flag, change only the rollout percentage, and decide from the code whether that user's numbers change.

excerpts.quote: export function bucket(flagKey: string, distinctId: string, salt = ""): number {

S14 closes the analytics loop: the product ships feature flags, and measures their effect with A/B experiments. Two design questions decide everything downstream: **how is a user assigned to a variant**, and **how do we decide an experiment worked**.

readMore.why: The evaluation order and the two salted draws.

notes.title: The window is measured from step 1, not the previous step
notes.body:
The view on day 0 sets `anchor` (funnel.ts:58). The signup on day 5 passes `t <= anchor + windowMs` (5 <= 7) and the level becomes 2. The purchase on day 9 is checked against the SAME anchor: 9 > 0 + 7, so it is rejected. The person counts at steps 1 and 2.

- "Within 7 days of the signup" is the rule Pulse deliberately did not choose; the doc calls the choice a product decision with revenue implications.
- "Only bounds the gap between neighbours" is the same mistake in other words.
- "The signup resets the anchor" is wrong: the anchor is only assigned while `level === 0`.

excerpts.quote: } else if (level < n && matchesStep(e, spec.steps[level]) && t <= anchor + windowMs) {
The window is measured from step 1**, not from the previous step.

notes.title: Why the window edge is inside the window
notes.body:
The check at funnel.ts:62 is `t <= anchor + windowMs`, with `<=`, not `<`, and it is the same check for every step after the first. A step at exactly anchor + 7 days therefore counts; one millisecond later fails. The contract states it the same way, so analysts and the code agree.

- "Half-open, ending just before" would need `<`.
- "Only for the last step, with a strict < for earlier steps" is wrong: there is a single comparison, and line 62 applies `<=` to every step after the first.
- "Rounded to whole days" is wrong: `windowMs` is `spec.windowDays * DAY_MS` and timestamps are compared in milliseconds.

excerpts.quote: const windowMs = spec.windowDays * DAY_MS;
A conversion at *exactly* anchor + window counts; one millisecond later
} else if (level < n && matchesStep(e, spec.steps[level]) && t <= anchor + windowMs) {

notes.title: Order matters: a step before its predecessor is ignored
notes.body:
Walk the events in time order. The day-0 signup comes first, while `level` is 0, and the only thing that can match at level 0 is step 1. So the signup is skipped. The day-1 view then sets the anchor and level 1. No later signup exists, so the person ends at level 1 and counts at step 1 only.

- "Order is ignored inside the window" contradicts rule 3: steps must occur in sequence.
- "The person is discarded" is wrong: reaching step 1 is enough to be counted as an entrant.
- "Counts at step 2" would need the signup to come AFTER the anchor.

excerpts.quote: if (level === 0) { if (matchesStep(e, spec.steps[0])) { anchor = t;
`B … A` does **not** — doing signup before your first view

notes.title: The earliest step-1 event is the only anchor
notes.body:
The anchor is written in one place, inside `if (level === 0)`. After the day-0 view, `level` is 1, so the day-6 view matches nothing the walker is looking for (it wants step 2) and is skipped. The signup on day 8 is compared with anchor 0: 8 > 7, rejected. The person stays at step 1.

- "The day-6 view re-anchors" describes a different funnel design (latest anchor); rule 1 says the earliest step-1 event anchors everything.
- "Any step-1 event within 7 days of the signup" is not a rule anywhere in the code.
- "A repeated step-1 event disqualifies the person" is wrong: they still count at step 1.

excerpts.quote: A person "enters" the funnel at their **earliest** step-1 event within the lookback

notes.title: A breakdown labels each person once
notes.body:
`computeFunnelBreakdown` first scans the events and, for each person, stores a label from the FIRST step-1 event it meets (`if (!labelOf.has(person))`). Then it puts every event of that person into that one group and runs a normal funnel per group. A person whose first view was on Firefox is in the Firefox group, even if all later events say Chrome.

One precision: "first" here means first in the order the events arrive in the input array. This loop does not sort; the time sort happens only inside `computeFunnel` (funnel.ts:50). With time-ordered input the two agree.

- "Both groups" would double-count people; the label map holds one label per person.
- "The majority browser" is not computed anywhere.
- "(none)" is only used when the property is missing or null on that first event.

excerpts.quote: if (!labelOf.has(person)) {
// Assign each person a breakdown label from their FIRST step-1 event's property.

notes.title: Why the flag key is part of the hash input
notes.body:
bucket() hashes the string `${flagKey}:${salt}:${distinctId}`. Because the flag key is in the input, flag A and flag B give a user two unrelated bucket values. Without it, every experiment would split users the same way: the people in "test" for one experiment would be in "test" for all of them, and their effects would be confounded. The property tests (chi-square and Pearson) exist to catch exactly that.

- "Move a user by editing the key" is a side effect of a new key (a new experiment), not the reason it is hashed.
- "Only a cache key" is wrong: the key is literally in the hashed string.
- "To make the hash slower" is wrong: FNV-1a is chosen for being cheap.

excerpts.quote: return hash32(`${flagKey}:${salt}:${distinctId}`) / 0x100000000;
the flagKey is IN the hash input, so experiments don't share a split.

notes.title: Ramping a rollout never moves existing users
notes.body:
The rollout gate is `bucket(flag.key, ctx.distinctId, "rollout") >= flag.rolloutPercentage / 100`. The draw depends on the key, the salt and the user, not on the percentage. A user whose draw was below 0.10 is also below 0.20, so they stay in; the ramp only admits users with draws between 0.10 and 0.20.

- "Reshuffled" would need the draw to change; nothing in its input changed.
- "Removed until a new assignment table" is wrong: there is no assignment table at all.
- "A new variant" is wrong too: the variant pick uses its own "variant" salt and the same inputs, so it is also unchanged.

To re-randomize on purpose you change the flag key, which starts a new experiment.

excerpts.quote: if (rolloutDraw >= flag.rolloutPercentage / 100) {
it never moves someone who was already in.

notes.title: evaluateFlag returns at the first check that fails
notes.body:
Read `evaluateFlag` top to bottom. It returns "disabled" if the flag is off. Next, if the flag has targeting filters and the user's properties do not match them all, it returns the control variant with reason "not_targeted". Only a targeted user reaches the rollout draw and can get "out_of_rollout". A user who fails targeting never gets that far, so the rollout result does not matter.

- "out_of_rollout" would need targeting to pass first.
- "disabled" is reserved for `!flag.enabled`; this flag is enabled.
- "rollout" is the reason for a user inside the rollout who gets a weighted variant.

excerpts.quote: return { flagKey: flag.key, variant: control, reason: "not_targeted" };

notes.title: Peeking turns a 5% test into a 26% one
notes.body:
Both arms of an A/A test share the same 10% conversion rate, so every "significant" result is false by construction. Checking after every 100 samples and stopping at the first p < 0.05 gives about 26% false positives in the simulation; one look at the planned sample size gives about 4.7%.

Why: a p-value is calibrated for ONE look. Each extra look is another chance for noise to cross the line, and the peeker stops exactly at that random high point.

- "About 5%" is the fixed-horizon rate, not the peeking rate.
- "About 50%" overstates the table.
- "Zero" confuses "the true lift is zero" with "no test can come out significant".

excerpts.quote: | **Peeking** | check p after every 100 samples, stop the first time p < 0.05 | **~26%** |
A p-value is calibrated for **one** look.

notes.title: Pooled for the test, separate variances for the interval
notes.body:
The z-test asks "could these two rates be equal?", so under that null hypothesis it pools them: `pooled = (c1 + c2) / (n1 + n2)` and the standard error uses that one rate. The confidence interval describes the difference we actually estimated, so it uses each arm's own variance: `seUnpooled` adds `rate * (1 - rate) / exposed` per arm.

- "Pooled for both" is wrong for the interval; the code comment says the CI deliberately uses the unpooled SE.
- "Unpooled for both" is wrong for the z-test.
- "Separate variances in the test, shared rate for the interval" is the exact reverse of the code.

excerpts.quote: const pooled = (c1 + c2) / (n1 + n2);
The lift CI uses the UNPOOLED SE (each

notes.title: The 60-second "undead key" window
notes.body:
Authenticating every `POST /e` with a database lookup would make auth the bottleneck, so the resolver caches the hash-to-key mapping in process. Each cache entry expires `ttlMs` after it was stored, and `ttlMs` defaults to 60_000. A key revoked in the database keeps working on that instance until its cached entry expires: at most 60 seconds. ADR-0003 states this cost on purpose.

- "Not at all" describes an instant cache-bust on revoke, which does not exist yet: the ADR only says the management side "can add an instant cache-bust later".
- "For the process lifetime" is wrong: entries have an expiry time.
- "24 hours" mixes in `lastUsedAt`, which is a ~1% sampled write and has nothing to do with expiry.

excerpts.quote: this.ttlMs = opts.ttlMs ?? 60_000;
**a revoked key keeps working for up to 60s** ("undead key")
management side can add an instant cache-bust later

notes.title: Working out a sampled estimate by hand
notes.body:
`estimateFromSample(400, 0.1)`: the estimate is round(400 / 0.1) = 4000, the observed count scaled up by the sample rate. The standard error is sqrt(400 * 0.9) / 0.1 = sqrt(360) / 0.1, about 189.7, and the 95% interval is 1.96 times that, about 372. `formatEstimate` shows that band relative to the estimate, 372 / 4000, about 9%.

- "~400 ±5%" forgets to scale the observed count up by the sample rate.
- "~4,000 exactly" misreads the reliability floor: 30 observed events only decides `reliable`; a sampled number is never shown without its ±.
- "~40,000 ±1%" divides by the square of the rate, which the code never does.

excerpts.quote: const se = Math.sqrt(observed * (1 - sampleRate)) / sampleRate;
**Never render a sampled number as exact.**

notes.title: The pipeline ADRs: storage, SDK, stream, identity and columns
notes.body:
The newer questions in this quest follow an event's whole journey through Pulse, one ADR at a time.

ADR-0002 is the starting storage decision and the way it planned for its own end. ADR-0004 is the contract for the browser SDK, a library that runs on other people's pages. ADR-0005 introduces the stream between ingest and storage, with a table mapping its terms onto Kafka. ADR-0006 decides how many anonymous and logged-in ids become one person. ADR-0007 records the move to a columnar store, and publishes the numbers of the options that lost.

For flashcards, ADR-0008 (compute or precompute), ADR-0012 (staying on the current transport) and the Sprint 13 audit fill in the rest.

Read each Rationale section slowly: it usually states the rule the decision follows, and the questions test whether you can apply that rule.

excerpts.quote: `@pulse/sdk` runs on pages we do not own, do not test, and cannot update on anyone's schedule.
Analytics sees a person through many ids: an anonymous browser id, then a logged-in user id, across devices.

readMore.why: The stream between ingest and storage, with its Kafka concept map.

notes.title: The three numeric exit criteria for leaving Postgres
notes.body:
ADR-0002 starts events on a naive Postgres table and writes down, in S01, the numbers at which that decision expires. Any one of three is enough: sustained ingest above about 2,000 events/sec pushing insert p95 above 50 ms; a trends or funnel query over more than about 50M events taking longer than about 2 s at p95; or the events table dominating size, vacuum and backup so that OLTP metadata suffers.

- There is no raw disk-size threshold; the operational criterion is about harm to the metadata, not gigabytes.
- The ingest criterion pairs ~2,000 events/sec with 50 ms, not ~500/sec with 2 s.
- The query criterion is ~50M events and ~2 s, not ~5M and 200 ms.

excerpts.quote: a trends/funnel query over **> ~50M events** exceeds **~2 s** p95

notes.title: Why the Event table is left under-optimized on purpose
notes.body:
ADR-0002's first consequence is that the `Event` table is deliberately under-optimized: one btree on `(projectId, ts)`, no partitioning, no BRIN and no columnar layout. Its reason is a teaching one: optimizing it now would blunt the S07 lesson, in which the load generator drives Pulse across the written exit criteria and the team then migrates the events store.

- No Postgres version limit is mentioned.
- The unique uuid index arrives later with the stream consumer (ADR-0005); it is not the reason here.
- The ADR makes no claim about what BRIN indexes can or cannot serve.

excerpts.quote: Optimizing it now would blunt the S07 lesson.

notes.title: Never break the host page, not even while reporting
notes.body:
ADR-0004's first principle runs every public SDK entry point inside a never-throw boundary called `guard`. Errors are swallowed and can be reported through `onError`, and that reporting call is itself wrapped, so a broken reporter cannot re-break the page. The stake is spelled out: a bug in analytics must never take down checkout.

- Rethrowing to the host would break the very principle the guard exists for.
- The ADR does not limit the reporter to development builds.
- Nothing batches errors with the next flush; flush triggers are about events.

excerpts.quote: the reporting is itself wrapped, so a broken reporter can't re-break the page.

notes.title: Why the event uuid must be born in the browser
notes.body:
ADR-0004 makes the browser mint each event's `uuid` at capture time, because it is the idempotency key the whole pipeline relies on: Sprint 04 dedupes on it, and the Sprint 07 backfill stays idempotent because of it. If the id were minted downstream, a network retry would arrive as a new event with a new id, and nothing could collapse the two.

- Collisions between browsers are not the concern raised.
- The beacon path's header limit is about where the write key goes, not about ids.
- Person lookup happens in the consumer via the mapping table and has nothing to do with where the uuid is minted.

excerpts.quote: Mint it downstream and a network retry becomes an uncollapsible duplicate.

notes.title: Asymmetric failure modes set the SDK's priorities
notes.body:
ADR-0004's rationale ranks the SDK's priorities: don't break the page, then deliver the event, then be small, then be featureful. The reason is asymmetry. A dropped event is a data gap; a thrown exception is a customer outage and a churned account. Every principle in the ADR falls out of that ordering.

- Delivery is second, not first: the ADR openly accepts some lost events in exchange for safety and size.
- Size is enforced in CI, but enforcement does not move it above delivery.
- Fast loading is not a separate priority that outranks delivery.

excerpts.quote: *don't break the page > deliver the event > be small > be featureful.*

notes.title: Good-citizen monkey-patching of history
notes.body:
Auto-pageview has to patch the page's `history` API, which the customer's own code and other vendors may also patch. ADR-0004 sets three rules. Compose with the original: call it first and return its result. Be idempotent: never double-patch. Be reversible: teardown restores the original exactly.

- Replacing the original would break the host's own navigation code.
- Proxies, async wrappers and sandboxes are not part of the rule.
- Running before the original is the opposite of calling it first, and a patch that is never torn down fails reversibility.

excerpts.quote: by composing with the original (call it first, return its result), idempotently (no double-patch), and reversibly (teardown restores it exactly).

notes.title: Keep the hot path dumb; put state work in the consumer
notes.body:
ADR-0005 splits ingestion in two. The hot path does as little as possible: validate cheaply and append to the stream. Everything stateful, meaning dedup against a unique index, enrichment and batching, happens in the consumer, because that is where the database and the batch already are. The rule is "place correctness where state already lives".

- The ingest handler is the hot path the ADR wants to keep dumb.
- The SDK mints the uuid used for dedup but does not dedupe anything itself.
- Query time is too late: duplicates would already be stored.

excerpts.quote: happens in the consumer where the database — and the batch — already are.

notes.title: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent apply
notes.body:
ADR-0005 treats delivery guarantees as a property of a pair, not of a transport. Redis Streams delivers at least once: if a consumer inserts and then crashes before XACK, the entries come back. Pulse makes that harmless by making the apply idempotent, with a unique `uuid` and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. The ADR asks you to memorize the result: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent apply equals effective exactly-once.

- Acking before inserting would lose the batch on a crash instead of repeating it.
- Redis itself does not drop repeated deliveries; that is the job of the apply.
- The SDK is not involved; this happens entirely between the stream and the database.

excerpts.quote: We make the *apply* idempotent (unique `uuid` + ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING)

notes.title: A merge fixes the future and leaves history alone
notes.body:
ADR-0006 resolves identity at write time: the consumer freezes `personId` onto each event row. The event log is immutable, and identity is a view over it through the `DistinctIdMapping` table. When `identify` merges two persons, the consumer moves the loser's mappings to the survivor, folds the loser's properties into it and deletes the loser's Person row. New lookups resolve to the survivor, while old event rows keep the personId they were written with. The ADR calls this the same append-only instinct as the stream and every ledger.

- Updating old event rows is exactly what the ADR forbids: history is never UPDATEd.
- No new combined person is created; one of the two survives.
- There is no nightly backfill that recomputes frozen ids.

excerpts.quote: A merge changes `DistinctIdMapping`, never event rows.

notes.title: Merging persons safely: a per-user lock and a fixed winner
notes.body:
An identify merge is a check-then-act on a shared id, so two concurrent identifies for one user could split them into two persons. ADR-0006 serializes them with a lock keyed on the user id (`pg_advisory_xact_lock` in production). For replays it picks a deterministic winner: the oldest person wins, so running the same identify twice ends in the same state.

- The lock is scoped to the user id, not the whole table.
- It is a lock, not an optimistic version check, and the winner is the oldest person, not the newest.
- Event counts and device identity do not decide the winner.

excerpts.quote: the **oldest person wins** (deterministic → a replayed identify is idempotent).

notes.title: Why Pulse will not guess that two devices are one person
notes.body:
ADR-0006 defers cross-device probabilistic matching and marks it "declined, probably forever". Its reason is about trust in one number: guessing that two ids belong to the same person silently corrupts "how many users?", the one number analytics must not lie about. Deterministic merges through identify are allowed because they are facts, not guesses.

- Speed on the write path is not the argument.
- The ADR does not cite browser privacy rules.
- The merge lock is keyed on a user id and has nothing to do with devices.

excerpts.quote: silently corrupts "how many users?", the one number analytics must not lie about.

notes.title: Why rollups lost to a columnar store
notes.body:
ADR-0007 publishes the loser's numbers. Partitioned Postgres with rollups reached about 3.1 s on rollup-able queries, but about 9 s on arbitrary-filter distinct counts. The reason: rollups can only precompute the questions you named in advance, while the product's strength is arbitrary filters and breakdowns. The moment a user filters by a property no rollup covers, they are scanning raw partitions again.

- The table lists that option's ingest as improved, not worse.
- No nightly rebuild or day-old data is mentioned.
- The weakness is ad-hoc filters, not an inability to count distinct persons.

excerpts.quote: rollups can only precompute the questions you named in advance

notes.title: The ORDER BY spine, and why uuid comes last
notes.body:
In ClickHouse, ADR-0007 says, the ORDER BY is the primary index, the locality and the compression all at once. `(projectId, name, ts)` comes first because nearly every insight filters on project, usually on name, and always on a time window.

Why uuid has to be in the key at all: `ReplacingMergeTree` treats rows that share the whole sorting key as copies of one row and keeps only one of them when parts merge. Without uuid, two genuinely different events with the same project, name and millisecond would be merged into one. With uuid last, only a true re-delivery of the same event shares the whole key. Merges are eventual, so the consumer also skips repeats it saw recently, with a bounded window of the last 100,000 uuids.

- Single-event lookup by uuid is not the goal; it is the last column of the spine.
- Partitions are by month of ts, not by uuid.
- ClickHouse enforces no unique index at insert time.

excerpts.quote: `uuid` last so `ReplacingMergeTree` can collapse exact re-deliveries.
the same sorting key at MERGE time (eventually), keeping the max `ingestedAt`.

notes.title: Acknowledged before it is stored: the buffered column store
notes.body:
Pulse's pipeline rests on one ordering: a consumer acknowledges a stream entry only after the event is stored, so a crash means redelivery rather than loss. Read the consumer as it runs after the ClickHouse cutover (`EVENTS_PRIMARY=ch`, no dual-write) and the order looks right: it awaits the column store's `insert`, then XACKs.

But the column store it was handed is a buffering wrapper. Its `insert` appends to an in-memory array and writes to ClickHouse only once 10,000 rows have piled up, and nothing in the consumer calls `flush` when the stream goes idle or the process drains for a deploy. A small batch is therefore acknowledged while it lives only in process memory. A crash or rollover before the buffer fills loses it for good, and on a quiet project the events may never reach ClickHouse at all.

- The awaited insert returns before ClickHouse has the rows.
- Postgres is not written in this mode.
- The XACK has already taken the entries off the pending list.

excerpts.quote: for (const e of events) if (this.isFreshUuid(e.uuid)) this.buffer.push(e); // insert-window dedupe
Post-decommission: ClickHouse IS the source of truth now
